# Passenger Rail Corridor Proposal: Albany, NY to Buffalo, NY

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This proposal evaluates three alignment alternatives for passenger rail service along the Albany, NY to Buffalo, NY corridor. The alternatives evaluated are Alternative 1 (Existing corridor upgrade), Alternative 2 (New direct alignment), and Alternative 3 (Maximum population served). Among these, Alternative 3 achieves the highest composite score of 85.6 out of 100 and reaches the highest population near line at 3.32 million residents across 5 stations. Alternative 1 offers the lowest median cost with a median (P50) of $6.9B and the shortest median schedule with a median (P50) of 13.6 years.

## Corridor Description

The corridor spans multiple routing choices assessed within a 10 miles population buffer. Alternative 1 (Existing corridor upgrade) covers 284 miles with a 100.0% share on existing rail, serving a population of 3.12 million near line across 4 stations: Buffalo, Syracuse, Albany, and Utica. Alternative 2 (New direct alignment) provides the shortest route at 275 miles with a 16.6% share on existing rail, reaching 2.77 million residents across 2 stations: Buffalo and Albany. Alternative 3 (Maximum population served) spans 315 miles with a 51.7% share on existing rail, serving 3.32 million residents near line across 5 stations: Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse, Albany, and Utica.

## Cost and Schedule Range

Capital costs are illustrative estimates, not budgets, derived from 5000 Monte Carlo simulation runs per route. For Alternative 1, capital cost ranges from P10 of $5.6B, median (P50) of $6.9B, to P90 of $8.6B, with delivery times of P10 of 11.7 years, median (P50) of 13.6 years, and P90 of 15.7 years. Alternative 2 reflects illustrative cost estimates of P10 of $10.8B, median (P50) of $13.0B, and P90 of $15.7B, with opening timelines of P10 of 13.1 years, median (P50) of 14.8 years, and P90 of 16.8 years. Alternative 3 has illustrative cost estimates of P10 of $10.9B, median (P50) of $13.1B, and P90 of $15.8B, with an expected timeline of P10 of 12.9 years, median (P50) of 14.7 years, and P90 of 16.7 years.

## Funding Strategy

The capital and planning strategy combines federal grant programs and federal loan options. Initial scoping relies on the Corridor Identification and Development Program (Corridor ID) via the FRA, providing $500K in planning support. The primary capital grant source is the FRA Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National), offering up to $3.0B per award, representing a federal share of median cost of 43.6% for Alternative 1, 23.1% for Alternative 2, and 22.8% for Alternative 3. Supplementary grant support includes FRA CRISI grants up to $250M (3.6% federal share of median cost for Alternative 1, 1.9% for Alternative 2 and 3) and USDOT BUILD grants up to $25M for station or discrete capital works. Non-federal matching requirements can be financed using the USDOT Build America Bureau RRIF loan program, providing up to $1.4B in loan funds for Alternative 1 or $2.6B for Alternative 2 and Alternative 3.

## Risks

Project risks differ based on right-of-way reuse and environmental features. Alternative 1 includes 15 environmental flag entries and 8 river crossings, requiring detailed engineering to manage existing rail constraints. Alternative 2 involves 3 environmental flag entries and 2 river crossings, presenting challenges associated with greenfield acquisition. Alternative 3 incorporates 7 environmental flag entries and 5 river crossings along its extended routing.

## Next Steps

Key next steps include entering Step 1 scoping through the Corridor Identification and Development Program using the allocated $500K federal planning match. State planners should advance environmental reviews to address environmental flag entries and river crossings identified along the chosen alignment. Finally, project sponsors should engage the FRA and USDOT Build America Bureau to structure phased grant applications under the Federal-State Partnership program and evaluate RRIF loan options.
